posts.title: Building a Synthwave Renderer in Pure CSS
posts.excerpt: Recreating the iconic sunset grid with repeating-linear-gradients and a single horizon line. No JavaScript, no canvas — just gradients and a lot of patience.
posts.content:
## The grid is just math

Every synthwave scene starts with a floor that recedes into infinity. In CSS you do not need a canvas for that — you need two `repeating-linear-gradient`s and a perspective trick that has been around since the dawn of the web.

The whole scene fits in three layers:

1. a **sky** gradient (deep indigo to near-black)
2. a **sun** made of one radial-gradient and a few horizontal slice masks
3. a **floor grid** with `transform: perspective()` and a slow upward scroll

```css
.floor {
  background-image:
    repeating-linear-gradient(90deg, transparent 0 39px, #7f8bb2 39px 40px),
    repeating-linear-gradient(0deg, transparent 0 39px, #7f8bb2 39px 40px);
  transform: perspective(200px) rotateX(60deg);
}
```

## Why bother

The constraints are the fun part. A renderer built from gradients weighs a few kilobytes, scales to any resolution, and degrades gracefully on machines that never had a GPU to begin with.

> Nostalgia is a rendering technique.

Next time I want to add palette cycling on top of this — a handful of CSS custom properties driven by a single `@keyframes` rule.

posts.title: Why I Still Write Assembly for Fun
posts.excerpt: There's a meditative quality to hand-optimising a loop. This post walks through a tiny demoscene effect written in x86-64, from registers to pixels.
posts.content:
## Registers are a kind of poetry

Modern compilers are better than me at almost everything. That is exactly why writing assembly by hand is still worth doing: not to beat the compiler, but to understand what it is doing.

My rule is simple — if a routine fits in a screen of text and touches the framebuffer, I will write it by hand at least once.

## A tiny effect

The effect: a vertical wipe that writes a colour ramp directly into video memory.

```asm
loop:
    mov  al, [rsi]
    mov  [rdi], al
    inc  rsi
    add  rdi, 4
    dec  rcx
    jnz  loop
```

Six instructions. No branches except the loop itself. On a modern CPU this runs at memory speed and the frame budget disappears entirely.

The point is not speed. The point is that after writing this, you can *see* the machine.

posts.title: RetroArch Setup for Pixel-Perfect Gaming
posts.excerpt: Integer scaling, shaders, and the right aspect ratio. A complete guide to making 240p games look exactly like they did on your childhood TV.
posts.content:
## Start with integer scaling

Non-integer scaling is the single biggest source of ugly pixels. Turn it on, accept the black bars, and never look back.

## Shaders

`crt-guest-advanced` is the current sweet spot between accuracy and performance. On a low-end machine, fall back to `crt-geom`.

## The checklist

- integer scale: **on**
- aspect ratio: **core provided**
- bilinear filtering: **off**
- frame delay: **1–2**

That is the entire setup. Everything else is taste.

posts.title: Demoscene Tricks: Dithering and Palette Cycling
posts.excerpt: Before shaders, we had ordered dithering and palette rotation. Revisiting the classic techniques that squeezed beauty out of 16 colors.
posts.content:
## 16 colours is enough

Ordered dithering is a magic trick: you trade spatial resolution for perceived colour depth, and the eye fills in the rest.

A 4×4 Bayer matrix is enough to make a two-colour image look like it has a dozen shades.

## Palette cycling

Instead of animating pixels, rotate the palette. It costs almost nothing and it produced some of the most memorable effects of the 90s.

```js
const cycle = palette.slice(1).concat(palette[0]);
```

Two lines of code, one entire aesthetic movement.

posts.title: A Terminal-Based Blog Engine in 200 Lines
posts.excerpt: Markdown to HTML via awk, a Makefile, and a pure-CGI script. The result is a fast, dependency-free blog that works in any text browser.
posts.content:
## Constraints as a feature

I wanted a blog I could update over SSH from a machine with no package manager. No Node, no Ruby, no build cache.

The answer was a 200-line CGI script, a `Makefile`, and a folder of `.md` files.

## How it works

1. `make` converts every Markdown file to HTML
2. the CGI script reads a directory index
3. the browser gets plain HTML

## The result

Loads in under 20ms on a Raspberry Pi. Works in `lynx`. Never needs an update. The only thing it cannot do is look cool, which is why this blog exists.
